bib.title: The No-U-Turn Sampler: Adaptively Setting Path Lengths in Hamiltonian Monte Carlo

question: Can HMC be made to run without hand-setting the number of leapfrog steps L and the step size epsilon, while sampling as efficiently as a well-tuned HMC?
hypothesis: A U-turn stopping criterion built by recursive doubling, plus dual-averaging step-size adaptation, gives tuning-free sampling at least as efficient as well-tuned HMC.
contributions: NUTS, an HMC extension that eliminates the number-of-steps parameter L via a recursive doubling and U-turn criterion
A dual averaging scheme for automatically tuning step size epsilon in both HMC and NUTS
Empirical comparison showing tuning-free NUTS matches or beats tuned HMC on four targets

method.summary: NUTS doubles a balanced binary tree of leapfrog states forwards or backwards until a subtree makes a U-turn (or energy error is huge), then samples uniformly from the valid slice states with a memory-efficient kernel. Epsilon is tuned during burn-in by Nesterov-style dual averaging toward a target acceptance statistic delta. NUTS and HMC are compared on ESS per gradient evaluation over a grid of delta and HMC simulation lengths, on four target distributions.
method.task: MCMC sampling of continuous posteriors (Bayesian inference)

datasets.name: 250-D multivariate normal (synthetic)
datasets.source: zero-mean, precision matrix A drawn from Wishart with identity scale and 250 degrees of freedom; same A in all experiments

datasets.name: German credit (Bayesian logistic regression, LR)
datasets.preprocessing: predictors normalized to zero mean and unit variance; N(0, sigma^2=100) priors on alpha and each beta

datasets.name: German credit hierarchical logistic regression (HLR)
datasets.size: 1000 customers; 300 predictors after two-way interactions, 300 coefficients plus alpha and sigma^2 (paper: sigma^2 interacts with the remaining 301 variables)
datasets.preprocessing: 24 choose 2 + 24 = 300-dim predictors; prior variance sigma^2 with Exponential prior rate lambda=0.01 (mean and sd 100)

datasets.name: Stochastic volatility (SV)
datasets.size: 3000 days of S&P 500 returns; 3001-dimensional target after integrating out tau
datasets.preprocessing: precision parameter tau integrated out; priors tau, nu, s1 ~ Exponential(100)

inference.samples: 2000 iterations per run (first 1000 burn-in and epsilon adaptation, last 1000 used); 10 random seeds per sampler x simulation-length x delta x target; 3,200 HMC runs and 600 NUTS runs in total

parameters.epsilon_1: FindReasonableEpsilon heuristic (Algorithm 4): double or halve until Langevin proposal acceptance crosses 0.5
parameters.HMC_simulation_lengths: 10 logarithmically spaced lambda per target; largest is 40x smallest (ratio 40^(1/9) ~ 1.5)
parameters.adaptation_statistic_HMC: H_t = delta - min(1, p(theta~,r~)/p(theta_{t-1}, r_{t,0})), x = log epsilon
parameters.adaptation_statistic_NUTS: H_t = delta - mean over states in final doubling of min(1, p(theta,r)/p(theta_{t-1},r_{t,0})), x = log epsilon
parameters.momentum: r ~ N(0, I); kinetic energy 0.5 r.r (no mass matrix)
parameters.gamma_t0_kappa_origin: chosen by hand on the stochastic volatility model with NUTS and HMC

other.qualitative_run: NUTS delta=0.5, 2000 iterations (1000 burn-in), about 1,000,000 gradient evaluations; RWM 1,000,000 iterations; Gibbs 1,000,000 sweeps; 250-D MVN

metrics.name: ESS per gradient evaluation
metrics.definition: Effective sample size of the 1000 post-burn-in samples divided by gradient evaluations used. ESS computed per dimension in terms of the variance of the estimator of the mean and of the second central moment (reference mean from a separate 50,000-iteration NUTS run with delta=0.5); the lower of the two, minimum across dimensions. Autocorrelation sum truncated when it first falls below 0.05.

metrics.name: h - delta
metrics.definition: Gap between realized average acceptance statistic h and its target delta, over the 1000 post-burn-in samples

baselines: HMC with dual averaging at 10 simulation lengths
eval.protocol: 10 seeds per configuration; gradient evaluations used as proxy for computation; results shown as plots (Fig 3-6), no significance tests stated.

availability.code: Matlab code at http://www.cs.princeton.edu/~mdhoffma; C++ implementation to be part of the soon-to-be-released Stan
availability.data: German credit from UCI; S&P 500 returns source not given

evidence.quote: We used the values γ = 0.05, t0 = 10, and κ = 0.75 for all our experiments.

results.claim: On the multivariate normal and stochastic volatility problems NUTS with delta=0.6 beats the best ESS per gradient of HMC by about a factor of three.
results.metric: ESS per gradient, NUTS / best HMC
results.setup: 250-D MVN and SV targets, delta=0.6, 2000 iterations, 1000 post-burn-in, 10 seeds; HMC best over 10 simulation lengths
results.quote:
NUTS with δ = 0.6 outperforms HMC’s best ESS by about a factor of
three.
results.note: read as plot summary in Fig 6; value stated in words ('three')

results.claim: Best HMC simulation lengths varied by about a factor of 100 across the four targets, so HMC needs preliminary runs.
results.setup: four targets; longest optimal lambda 17.62 (MVN), shortest 0.17 (logistic regression)
results.quote: varied by about a factor of 100

results.claim: On the two logistic regression problems NUTS is about as efficient as HMC.
results.setup: LR and HLR, German credit, delta=0.6

results.claim: HMC's best ESS per gradient occurs around delta=0.65; NUTS's around 0.6 and is flat for delta in [0.45, 0.65].
results.setup: HMC across four targets; NUTS best near 0.6
results.quote:
HMC’s best performance
seems to occur around δ = 0.65

results.claim: Dual averaging usually coerces the acceptance statistic h to target delta, worse on stochastic volatility due to longer burn-in; averaged epsilon converges within a few hundred iterations except on SV.
results.setup: NUTS delta=0.65 for Fig 4; h computed from 1000 post-burn-in samples

results.claim: Most NUTS trajectory lengths are integer powers of two, so the U-turn criterion is usually met only after a doubling completes; length grows with delta.
On a 250-D correlated normal, NUTS with about 1,000,000 gradient evaluations generates many effectively independent samples, while RWM and Gibbs with 1,000,000 iterations barely explore.
results.setup: 250-D MVN, NUTS delta=0.5, 2000 iters; RWM isotropic proposal at acceptance 0.234; Gibbs 1,000,000 sweeps; qualitative comparison
results.quote: This required about 1,000,000 gradient and likelihood evaluations in total.

results.claim: HMC costs roughly O(D^(5/4)) per independent sample versus O(D^2) for random-walk Metropolis.
Theoretically optimal HMC average Metropolis acceptance probability is about 0.65.
results.setup: fixed simulation length epsilon*L, fairly strong assumptions

limits: Compared only against basic HMC, not extensions (mass matrix, windowed HMC, RMHMC).
Only simple kinetic energy 0.5 r.r; no mass matrix.
Only continuous differentiable unconstrained variables; discrete variables must be summed out or handled by Gibbs.
Dual averaging constants chosen by hand on the SV model; may not transfer to other samplers or statistics H.
Adaptation less accurate on SV because burn-in is long.
Comparison on ESS per gradient evaluation, ignoring wall-clock and tree-building overhead (argued negligible).
Only four targets; no significance tests; qualitative RWM and Gibbs comparison.

code.snippet: x_{t+1} <- mu - (sqrt(t)/gamma) * (1/(t+t0)) * sum_{i=1..t} H_i ; xbar_{t+1} <- eta_t x_{t+1} + (1-eta_t) xbar_t, eta_t = t^-kappa
FindReasonableEpsilon: init epsilon=1, r~N(0,I); a=2*I[p(theta',r')/p(theta,r)>0.5]-1; while (p'/p)^a > 2^-a: epsilon <- 2^a epsilon
